messages.author: 4b4a7b00c1dd09c7
messages.subject: Re: novice question too
parts:
Hi Sam,

On Fri, 02 Jun 2000 15:36:28, Samantha Lake wrote:

> >We are conducting a series of surveys of Weddell seals hauled out on the
> >Antarctic fastice. We want to show seasonal changes in their abundance. My
> >question is whether to repeatedly survey the same set of randomly-placed
> >transects, or whether we should take a new set of randomly-placed transects
> >at each time interval.

By repeatedly surveying the same sites you increase your power (or
equivalent) to examine seasonal changes by cutting out one component of
variance (that due to re-sampling of sites). However, it becomes all the
more important to use a survey design that tends to produce good spatial
coverage (a "representative" sample of sites).

I think these issues are discussed extensively in the literature, in both
books on sampling and monitoring and in various papers in the biological
literature. For example:

Van der Meer, J. 1997. Sampling design of monitoring programmes for marine
benthos: a comparison between the use of fixed versus randomly selected
stations. Journal of Sea Research 37: 167-179.

Urquhart, N.S. et al. 1998. Monitoring for policy-relevant regional trends
over time. Ecological applications 8(2): 246-257.

Perhaps others can provide you with more references, if you don't have access
to literature search facilities.

Cheers,

- Len

P.S. What is a fastice?

--
Len Thomas (l...@mcs.st-and.ac.uk)
Research Unit for Wildlife Population Assessment
Mathematical Institute, University of St Andrews
Scotland
